messages.author: b29c64ed8b35851c
messages.subject: multivariate analysis
parts:
Hi all,

I have a dataset with a scalar dependent variable and several scalar,
ordinal, and nominal independent variables, and I'm not sure what type
of analysis to apply.

I'm looking at English comparative forms, which can be either
morphological (prouder) or periphrastic (more proud). I'd like to
predict the ratio of morphological and periphrastic comparisons for a
number of adjectives, as in the examples below:

broad (1403 morphological / 7 periphrastic = 200.42)
able (5 morphological / 171 periphrastic = 0.029)

The independent variables include things like frequency of the
positive adjective form, number of syllables, whether the final
phoneme is a syllabic consonant, etc.

Any suggestions will be greatly appreciated!

--Martin

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] multivariate analysis
parts:
Hi Martin,

this is the classic scenario for linear regression, but ...

>
> broad (1403 morphological / 7 periphrastic = 200.42)
> able (5 morphological / 171 periphrastic = 0.029)
>

... how many adjectives will you be looking at? I'm worrying a bit that
you might not have enough observations for reliable statistical analysis
if you aggregate your data in this way. It also sounds as though you're
planning to consider quite a few independent variables (which makes the
problem worse) ...

-Ben

messages.author: 5c92383d593d2a9a
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] multivariate analysis
parts:
> I'm looking at English comparative forms, which can be either
> morphological (prouder) or periphrastic (more proud). I'd like to
> predict the ratio of morphological and periphrastic comparisons for a
> number of adjectives, as in the examples below:
>
> broad (1403 morphological / 7 periphrastic = 200.42)
> able (5 morphological / 171 periphrastic = 0.029)

As Benedikt already pointed out, aggregating the data wouldn't
necessarily be the best choice.
You can, however, predict the ratio relatively easily as follows.

Use a Generalized Linear Model, with "periphrastic" as dichotomous
response variable. You can investigate its distribution or assume a
binomial one ("family=binomial(link=logit)").

Some of your independents may warrant a transformation (e.g. a log
transform for frequency), for others you may need to ensure that R
understands that they are factors.

I would probably use a mixed effects model and do a "by item"
analysis by specifying items as grouping variable (in the random
effects term). You may also want to specify subjects, if that
information is available.

Useful functions here are "lmer" and "glmmPQL" (MASS library).

The response that is predicted is actually the probability of a
periphrastic construction in that case. Because the GLM uses a link
function to transform this before fitting the actual model, you would
have to back-transform it (which is easy) should you actually wish to
predict the probability for a given combination of independents. But
possibly you're more interested in which predictors show significant
correlations - use summary(model) to find out (in particular with
glmmPQL).
Model-building may be necessary in that case (for example, starting
from the maximal model) - I found the explanations in Michael
Crawley's book (Wiley, 2005) quite helpful.

I hope that helps!


--

messages.author: 3edc58ee737edd94
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Re: multivariate analysis
parts:
Hi

I would imagine that regular linear regression runs into problems here
because a linear regression will generate values of the dependent
variable that lie outside the range of permissible values. For
example, if the dependent variable is the percentage of morphological
comparisons out of all morphological comparisons AND periphrastic
cases, then the dep. var. cannot take on negative values, which the
regression equation will predict. Same for when the dep. var. is the
ratio of the two comparison forms ... In addition, I wonder whether
the usual assumptions of linear regressions are met.

I think a binary logistic regression could be more useful here. The
dep. var. would be a two-column matrix of successed and failures set
up with cbind, and then one can use that matrix as a dep. var. in a
call for a glm with "family=binomial" as discussed in a previous
discussion on this list. This at least is the way tht Crawley (2005)
and Faraway (2005) discuss similar cases

Just my two cents ...
STG
